citation: Chow, M. (2016). Determinants of presence in 3D virtual worlds: A structural equation modelling analysis. Australasian Journal of Educational Technology, 32(1), 1-18.
discipline: nursing education / educational technology (technology-acceptance & presence research)
thesis: Presence research disproportionately studies technology-side determinants (immersion, interactivity, perceptual realism) while user-characteristic determinants remain understudied, despite presence being a psychological state of the user; Chow tests a structural-equation model in which subjective norm, perceived ease of use, and computer self-efficacy predict perceived usefulness, and perceived usefulness together with computer self-efficacy directly predict self presence, among 185 nursing students in a Second Life PPE-training simulation, framing the result as an initial, empirically validated model of individually-determined presence antecedents (FE, p.1, p.4, p.6-7, p.16).

sections.title: Introduction
sections.summary: Frames 3D virtual worlds as an educational platform and states the study's user-characteristics gap: most presence research emphasizes technology/immersive determinants over user-side determinants.

sections.title: The concept of presence
sections.summary: Surveys Lombard & Ditton's (1997) six explications and 'perceptual illusion of non-mediation' definition, then Lee's (2004) physical/social/self presence typology; narrows focus to self presence; situates presence as a human reaction to immersion (Slater).

sections.title: Presence and learning in virtual 3D environments
sections.summary: Reviews prior presence-learning findings (Mikropoulos & Natsis; Selverian & Hwang; Mikropoulos 2006); motivates the PPE-in-SL design via clinical-placement constraints in nursing education.

sections.title: Determinants of presence
sections.summary: Introduces the study's own two-category framework — media characteristics (form/content) vs. user characteristics (cognitive/emotional/motivational) — arguing the latter is understudied.

sections.title: Methodology — virtual world environment
sections.summary: Describes the custom Second Life PPE simulation: virtual dressing room, ten-room ward, sequenced donning/doffing tasks, automated performance log.

sections.title: Methodology — research model and hypotheses
sections.summary: Derives the model from Dunnington's (2012) NDPM and Davis's (1989) TAM; states five hypotheses (H1-H5) linking SN, PEOU, CSE to PU, and PU/CSE to presence.

sections.title: Methodology — instrument, sample and data collection
sections.summary: 14-item, 7-point-Likert instrument across five constructs adapted from validated scales; N=185 undergraduate nursing students.

sections.title: Data analysis and results
sections.summary: Two-step SEM (AMOS 19.0): measurement model then structural model, both good fit; all five hypotheses supported at p<.001.

sections.title: Discussion and Conclusions
sections.summary: Interprets CSE's dominant effect via Sweller's cognitive load theory; discusses PU/SN roles; states limitations (single-institution, cross-sectional, self-selected sample); frames the model as a first step.

constructs.label: embodiment / self-representation
constructs.treatment: sole dependent construct; Lee's (2004) self presence, operationalized via three avatar-motor-correspondence items; PU and CSE jointly explain 52% of its variance

constructs.label: self-efficacy
constructs.treatment: computer self-efficacy (CSE); direct antecedent of PU and of presence; strongest total predictor of presence (0.53)

constructs.label: cognitive load (extraneous vs germane)
constructs.treatment: not an SEM variable; post-hoc Sweller-derived explanation for CSE's dominant effect via extraneous-load-on-interface-navigation

constructs.label: presence (spatial/physical)
constructs.treatment: typological backdrop only (Lee's tripartite division); not modeled or measured

constructs.label: social presence / co-presence
constructs.treatment: typological backdrop only; explicitly excluded from the study's self-presence focus

constructs.label: affect: enjoyment & intrinsic motivation
constructs.treatment: mentioned only via a cited prior finding (deByl 2009) in the lit review; no affect/motivation construct in Chow's own SEM

constructs.label: representational fidelity
constructs.treatment: named as part of the 'media characteristics' determinant category, then set aside as already well-studied so the paper can focus on user characteristics

constructs.label: learning outcomes: procedural / skills
constructs.treatment: design intent only — PPE simulation built as a skills trainer with a performance log — but no skills/performance data collected; presence is the sole DV

conditions.label: desktop-3D / non-immersive VR
conditions.design: single-group, cross-sectional; custom Second Life PPE-training simulation (virtual dressing room + 10-room ward), desktop-accessed, no HMD; no comparison condition
conditions.sample: undergraduate nursing students, ages 20-24, 67.6% female; 12% first-year, 65% second-year, 23% final-year; 65% with no prior 3D-game/animation experience; single institution, voluntary/self-selected
conditions.instruments: 14-item, 7-point Likert survey: SN (2 items, Taylor & Todd 1995), PEOU (3 items, Venkatesh & Davis 2000), CSE (2 items, Vijayasarathy 2004), PU (4 items, Venkatesh & Davis 2000), self presence (3 items, Jin & Park 2009)
conditions.analysis: two-step SEM (AMOS 19.0): CFA measurement model then structural model
conditions.modelFit: measurement model chi2/df=1.78, RMSEA=.06, NFI=.96, NNFI=.97, CFI=.98; structural model chi2/df=1.74, RMSEA=.06, NFI=.96, NNFI=.97, CFI=.98; reliability alpha .81-.94; AVE>.50 throughout
conditions.effectDirection: all 5 hypotheses supported p<.001; SN(.32)+PEOU(.44)+CSE(.21) -> 65% variance in PU; PU(.36)+CSE(.45 direct/.53 total) -> 52% variance in self presence; CSE strongest total predictor

conditions.label: SEM / process model (no media contrast)
conditions.design: no between-media or between-group comparison arm; single desktop-3D condition modeled as a nomological network of antecedent-to-outcome paths, not a media-comparison design

readings.claim: Computer self-efficacy has the strongest direct and total effect on self presence of any variable in the model, exceeding perceived usefulness.
Perceived ease of use is the strongest predictor of perceived usefulness, followed by subjective norm, then computer self-efficacy.
All five hypothesized paths (SN->PU, PEOU->PU, CSE->PU, CSE->presence, PU->presence) are statistically supported.
Cognitive load theory (Sweller) explains CSE's dominant effect: low computer self-efficacy consumes cognitive resources on interface navigation, leaving fewer resources for immersion.

Because presence depends heavily on user confidence and perceived value, designers/educators should invest in orientation sessions and support to build computer self-efficacy rather than relying solely on technological fidelity.
The model is a first test only, limited by single-institution, cross-sectional, and voluntary/self-selected sampling, needing experimental follow-up.

concepts.term: Nature and Determinants of Presence Model (NDPM)

interlocutors.name: Lombard, Matthew & Theresa Ditton (= ped-sec-01)
interlocutors.role: source of the six explications of presence and the 'perceptual illusion of non-mediation' definition opening the lit review

interlocutors.name: Lee, Kwan Min
interlocutors.role: source of the physical/social/self presence typology; Chow adopts self presence as the study's focus construct

interlocutors.name: Slater, Mel
interlocutors.role: cited for 'presence is a human reaction to immersion,' distinguishing immersion (objective) from presence (subjective)

interlocutors.name: Sweller, John
interlocutors.role: cognitive load theory supplies the Discussion's explanation for CSE's dominant effect

interlocutors.name: Davis, Fred D.
interlocutors.role: originator of TAM; source of the PU/PEOU belief pair Chow imports as the study's core mechanism

interlocutors.name: Dunnington, Regina M.
interlocutors.role: author of the NDPM, the grounded-theory framework Chow's research model is explicitly derived from

interlocutors.name: Witmer, Jerome & Singer (2005 factor-structure paper)
interlocutors.role: cited only as one of several 'key authors of presence'; NOT the 1998 Presence Questionnaire paper built in this cluster as ped-sec-02 — Chow never cites the 1998 paper directly

tensions.axis: technology-determined presence (Witmer & Singer's Control/Sensory/Distraction/Realism, ped-sec-02) vs. psychologically/individually-determined presence (Chow's SN/PEOU/CSE/PU)
tensions.note: (P/anticipatory-application) This cluster's own debate-axis-3 construction; Chow does not cite Witmer & Singer's 1998 paper directly, only their 2005 follow-up.

tensions.axis: self presence (Chow's own focus) vs. social presence / co-presence (Lee's other type, and Strand F's primary construct)
tensions.note: Chow explicitly narrows to self presence and sets social presence aside; the two literatures should not be silently merged.

tensions.axis: presence as a variable predicted from user-side antecedents (Chow's NDPM/TAM-derived approach) vs. presence as a function of media/immersion level (Strand C's later media-comparison designs)
tensions.note: (P/anticipatory-application) Methodologically distinct traditions within the same construct space; useful for different claims, not interchangeable.

tensions.axis: Dunnington's broader NDPM (pedagogical + individual + group factors, plus a centricity mediator and learning-outcome endpoint) vs. Chow's own narrower, TAM-derived four-variable model (no pedagogical factors, no centricity measure, no learning-outcome data)
tensions.note: Chow presents the study's model as a simplified, testable instantiation of NDPM's individual/group categories, not a full test of NDPM itself.
